case_info.scenario: A 39-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer treated with anti-ERBB2 (formerly HER2) chemotherapy (ado-trastuzumab emtansine) presented to the emergency department with acute onset paralysis. Earlier that day she had upper-back muscle spasms while gardening. A few hours later, she developed weakness of both hands and legs, followed by urinary retention and saddle anesthesia. On arrival to the emergency department, the patient was febrile but hemodynamically stable. On physical examination, she had areflexia and weakness affecting all 4 limbs, with a sensory deficit distal to the T4 dermatome. Proprioception and vibratory sensation were intact throughout. Speech, comprehension, and cranial nerves were intact. Laboratory test results revealed elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, including white and red blood cell counts, protein and glucose levels, infectious studies, and cytologic testing, was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the total spine showed vertebral body metastases unchanged from a computed tomography scan obtained 8 months prior (Figure 1), multiple areas of new leptomeningeal enhancement around the distal spinal cord, and tumor infiltration of multiple vertebral bodies. An electromyogram showed grossly preserved motor conduction in the upper and lower extremities. F wave latencies (a measure of nerve conduction velocity between the spine and limb) were undetectable in the upper extremities and were normal in the lower extremities, suggesting upper motor neuron disease. Sensory conduction amplitudes of upper and lower extremity peripheral nerves were mildly decreased.
case_info.caption: A sagittal magnetic resonance imaging scan with contrast shows areas of metastatic breast cancer to the lumbar vertebral bodies, and the arrowheads show leptomeningeal spread.
case_info.explanation: Spinal cord infarct is a devastating syndrome characterized by abrupt symptom onset and accounts for 5% to 8% of acute myelopathy.1At presentation, 72% of patients with spinal cord infarct have associated back or limb pain at the level of involvement. This patient lost motor function and reflexes at the level of the infarct (C6 and C7) and had a loss of sensation at T4, but proprioception and vibratory sensation were maintained throughout the spine. These are hallmark examination findings of disruption of the anterior spinal artery, which supplies the anterior (but not posterior) spinal columns. The cervical plexus (C1 through C4) likely provided redundant innervation to the patient’s upper trunk, accounting for the T4 sensory deficit distal to the infarct. Only 24% of patients with spinal cord infarct have an abnormal MRI at the time of presentation, with most infarctions appearing as myelomalacia (radiographic “softening” of the spinal cord) on subsequent imaging (Figure 2).2Spinal cord infarct is thus largely a clinical diagnosis. Although more typically a result of a perioperative complication, this patient’s anterior spinal artery was likely disrupted by either direct invasion by breast cancer or by a thromboembolic event. Spinal cord infarct is treated with supportive care and reversal of the inciting process when possible. This patient was treated with oral and intrathecal chemotherapy, anticoagulation, and physical therapy; she had modest improvement in strength during a 2-month period. Spinal cord infarct has an estimated 3-year mortality rate of 23% and a wheelchair dependence rate of 42%.3 Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acquired autoimmune peripheral demyelinating disease. This uncommon syndrome (incidence of 1 to 2 per 100 000 people) can be triggered by infection and hematologic cancer.4Weakness owing to GBS progresses over weeks in an ascending fashion, with absent deep tendon reflexes seen in virtually all patients. Cerebrospinal fluid cytoalbuminologic dissociation (elevation of protein level with normal white blood cell count) is present in approximately two-thirds of patients with GBS and may take 1 week to develop. Although this patient was areflexic, the acute onset of her symptoms and preserved motor conduction on electromyogram do not support a diagnosis of GBS. Leptomeningeal disease (LMD) is found at autopsy in 20% of patients with metastatic cancer, and breast cancer is the solid tumor most likely to spread to the leptomeninges.5Multiple areas of involvement are common, and presenting symptoms, which correspond to areas of spinal involvement, are often heterogenous and multifocal. Spine MRI is 76% sensitive for the detection of LMD, demonstrating enhancement of the spinal cord or cauda equina.6Cerebrospinal fluid cytologic testing is only 54% sensitive with the first sample; however, only 3% of patients with LMD have completely normal CSF.7Common CSF findings include elevated protein level, decreased glucose level, and white blood cell pleocytosis (most commonly lymphocytosis). Although this patient had leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI, these areas did not correspond to her upper extremity neurologic deficits. The unremarkable CSF analysis further excluded paralysis owing to LMD. Although few medications are associated with acute onset quadriparesis, it is important to be mindful of potential drug adverse effects in patients with cancer. Adverse effects associated with ado-trastuzumab emtansine could explain some of the findings in this case, including peripheral neuropathy (shown on electromyogram) and muscle pain, but not paralysis.

The acute onset of paralysis, along with the MRI evidence of leptomeningeal enhancement and vertebral body metastases, suggests that the patient's symptoms are a result of compression of the spinal cord due to tumor infiltration. Immediate intervention, likely including corticosteroids or surgical decompression, is warranted to prevent further neurological deterioration.

dialogue_history.text: While compressive myelopathy is a valid concern, the presentation includes key features that argue against a purely structural cause: areflexia, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, and undetectable F waves in the upper extremities with normal motor conduction suggest an acute inflammatory or immune-mediated process, such as transverse myelitis, especially given the elevated inflammatory markers and history of immunomodulatory therapy. Given the unremarkable CSF and preserved proprioception/vibration, the priority should be urgent MRI with contrast of the entire neuroaxis and initiation of high-dose IV corticosteroids for suspected inflammatory myelopathy while arranging neurosurgical consultation for potential decompression if compression is confirmed.

3 = Moderate workload

  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

F wave latencies (a measure of nerve conduction velocity between the spine and limb) were undetectable in the upper extremities and were normal in the lower extremities, suggesting upper motor neuron disease. case_info.explanation: Spinal cord infarct is a devastating syndrome characterized by abrupt symptom onset and accounts for 5% to 8% of acute myelopathy.1At presentation, 72% of patients with spinal cord infarct have associated back or limb pain at the level of involvement. This patient lost motor function and reflexes at the level of the infarct (C6 and C7) and had a loss of sensation at T4, but proprioception and vibratory sensation were maintained throughout the spine. These are hallmark examination findings of disruption of the anterior spinal artery, which supplies the anterior (but not posterior) spinal columns. The cervical plexus (C1 through C4) likely provided redundant innervation to the patient’s upper trunk, accounting for the T4 sensory deficit distal to the infarct. Only 24% of patients with spinal cord infarct have an abnormal MRI at the time of presentation, with most infarctions appearing as myelomalacia (radiographic “softening” of the spinal cord) on subsequent imaging (Figure 2).2Spinal cord infarct is thus largely a clinical diagnosis. Although more typically a result of a perioperative complication, this patient’s anterior spinal artery was likely disrupted by either direct invasion by breast cancer or by a thromboembolic event. Spinal cord infarct is treated with supportive care and reversal of the inciting process when possible. This patient was treated with oral and intrathecal chemotherapy, anticoagulation, and physical therapy; she had modest improvement in strength during a 2-month period. Spinal cord infarct has an estimated 3-year mortality rate of 23% and a wheelchair dependence rate of 42%.3 Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acquired autoimmune peripheral demyelinating disease. This uncommon syndrome (incidence of 1 to 2 per 100 000 people) can be triggered by infection and hematologic cancer.4Weakness owing to GBS progresses over weeks in an ascending fashion, with absent deep tendon reflexes seen in virtually all patients. Cerebrospinal fluid cytoalbuminologic dissociation (elevation of protein level with normal white blood cell count) is present in approximately two-thirds of patients with GBS and may take 1 week to develop. Although this patient was areflexic, the acute onset of her symptoms and preserved motor conduction on electromyogram do not support a diagnosis of GBS. Leptomeningeal disease (LMD) is found at autopsy in 20% of patients with metastatic cancer, and breast cancer is the solid tumor most likely to spread to the leptomeninges.5Multiple areas of involvement are common, and presenting symptoms, which correspond to areas of spinal involvement, are often heterogenous and multifocal. Spine MRI is 76% sensitive for the detection of LMD, demonstrating enhancement of the spinal cord or cauda equina.6Cerebrospinal fluid cytologic testing is only 54% sensitive with the first sample; however, only 3% of patients with LMD have completely normal CSF.7Common CSF findings include elevated protein level, decreased glucose level, and white blood cell pleocytosis (most commonly lymphocytosis). Although this patient had leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI, these areas did not correspond to her upper extremity neurologic deficits. The unremarkable CSF analysis further excluded paralysis owing to LMD. Although few medications are associated with acute onset quadriparesis, it is important to be mindful of potential drug adverse effects in patients with cancer. Adverse effects associated with ado-trastuzumab emtansine could explain some of the findings in this case, including peripheral neuropathy (shown on electromyogram) and muscle pain, but not paralysis.

On physical examination, she had areflexia and weakness affecting all 4 limbs, with a sensory deficit distal to the T4 dermatome. Proprioception and vibratory sensation were intact throughout. Speech, comprehension, and cranial nerves were intact. Laboratory test results revealed elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, including white and red blood cell counts, protein and glucose levels, infectious studies, and cytologic testing, was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the total spine showed vertebral body metastases unchanged from a computed tomography scan obtained 8 months prior (Figure 1), multiple areas of new leptomeningeal enhancement around the distal spinal cord, and tumor infiltration of multiple vertebral bodies. An electromyogram showed grossly preserved motor conduction in the upper and lower extremities. F wave latencies (a measure of nerve conduction velocity between the spine and limb) were undetectable in the upper extremities and were normal in the lower extremities, suggesting upper motor neuron disease. Sensory conduction amplitudes of upper and lower extremity peripheral nerves were mildly decreased.

case_info.explanation: Spinal cord infarct is a devastating syndrome characterized by abrupt symptom onset and accounts for 5% to 8% of acute myelopathy.1At presentation, 72% of patients with spinal cord infarct have associated back or limb pain at the level of involvement. This patient lost motor function and reflexes at the level of the infarct (C6 and C7) and had a loss of sensation at T4, but proprioception and vibratory sensation were maintained throughout the spine. These are hallmark examination findings of disruption of the anterior spinal artery, which supplies the anterior (but not posterior) spinal columns. The cervical plexus (C1 through C4) likely provided redundant innervation to the patient’s upper trunk, accounting for the T4 sensory deficit distal to the infarct. Only 24% of patients with spinal cord infarct have an abnormal MRI at the time of presentation, with most infarctions appearing as myelomalacia (radiographic “softening” of the spinal cord) on subsequent imaging (Figure 2).2Spinal cord infarct is thus largely a clinical diagnosis. Although more typically a result of a perioperative complication, this patient’s anterior spinal artery was likely disrupted by either direct invasion by breast cancer or by a thromboembolic event. Spinal cord infarct is treated with supportive care and reversal of the inciting process when possible. This patient was treated with oral and intrathecal chemotherapy, anticoagulation, and physical therapy; she had modest improvement in strength during a 2-month period. Spinal cord infarct has an estimated 3-year mortality rate of 23% and a wheelchair dependence rate of 42%.3 Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acquired autoimmune peripheral demyelinating disease. This uncommon syndrome (incidence of 1 to 2 per 100 000 people) can be triggered by infection and hematologic cancer.4Weakness owing to GBS progresses over weeks in an ascending fashion, with absent deep tendon reflexes seen in virtually all patients. Cerebrospinal fluid cytoalbuminologic dissociation (elevation of protein level with normal white blood cell count) is present in approximately two-thirds of patients with GBS and may take 1 week to develop. Although this patient was areflexic, the acute onset of her symptoms and preserved motor conduction on electromyogram do not support a diagnosis of GBS. Leptomeningeal disease (LMD) is found at autopsy in 20% of patients with metastatic cancer, and breast cancer is the solid tumor most likely to spread to the leptomeninges.5Multiple areas of involvement are common, and presenting symptoms, which correspond to areas of spinal involvement, are often heterogenous and multifocal. Spine MRI is 76% sensitive for the detection of LMD, demonstrating enhancement of the spinal cord or cauda equina.6Cerebrospinal fluid cytologic testing is only 54% sensitive with the first sample; however, only 3% of patients with LMD have completely normal CSF.7Common CSF findings include elevated protein level, decreased glucose level, and white blood cell pleocytosis (most commonly lymphocytosis). Although this patient had leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI, these areas did not correspond to her upper extremity neurologic deficits. The unremarkable CSF analysis further excluded paralysis owing to LMD. Although few medications are associated with acute onset quadriparesis, it is important to be mindful of potential drug adverse effects in patients with cancer. Adverse effects associated with ado-trastuzumab emtansine could explain some of the findings in this case, including peripheral neuropathy (shown on electromyogram) and muscle pain, but not paralysis.

case_info.explanation: Spinal cord infarct is a devastating syndrome characterized by abrupt symptom onset and accounts for 5% to 8% of acute myelopathy.1At presentation, 72% of patients with spinal cord infarct have associated back or limb pain at the level of involvement. This patient lost motor function and reflexes at the level of the infarct (C6 and C7) and had a loss of sensation at T4, but proprioception and vibratory sensation were maintained throughout the spine. These are hallmark examination findings of disruption of the anterior spinal artery, which supplies the anterior (but not posterior) spinal columns. The cervical plexus (C1 through C4) likely provided redundant innervation to the patient’s upper trunk, accounting for the T4 sensory deficit distal to the infarct. Only 24% of patients with spinal cord infarct have an abnormal MRI at the time of presentation, with most infarctions appearing as myelomalacia (radiographic “softening” of the spinal cord) on subsequent imaging (Figure 2).2Spinal cord infarct is thus largely a clinical diagnosis. Although more typically a result of a perioperative complication, this patient’s anterior spinal artery was likely disrupted by either direct invasion by breast cancer or by a thromboembolic event. Spinal cord infarct is treated with supportive care and reversal of the inciting process when possible. This patient was treated with oral and intrathecal chemotherapy, anticoagulation, and physical therapy; she had modest improvement in strength during a 2-month period. Spinal cord infarct has an estimated 3-year mortality rate of 23% and a wheelchair dependence rate of 42%.3 Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acquired autoimmune peripheral demyelinating disease. This uncommon syndrome (incidence of 1 to 2 per 100 000 people) can be triggered by infection and hematologic cancer.4Weakness owing to GBS progresses over weeks in an ascending fashion, with absent deep tendon reflexes seen in virtually all patients. Cerebrospinal fluid cytoalbuminologic dissociation (elevation of protein level with normal white blood cell count) is present in approximately two-thirds of patients with GBS and may take 1 week to develop. Although this patient was areflexic, the acute onset of her symptoms and preserved motor conduction on electromyogram do not support a diagnosis of GBS. Leptomeningeal disease (LMD) is found at autopsy in 20% of patients with metastatic cancer, and breast cancer is the solid tumor most likely to spread to the leptomeninges.5Multiple areas of involvement are common, and presenting symptoms, which correspond to areas of spinal involvement, are often heterogenous and multifocal. Spine MRI is 76% sensitive for the detection of LMD, demonstrating enhancement of the spinal cord or cauda equina.6Cerebrospinal fluid cytologic testing is only 54% sensitive with the first sample; however, only 3% of patients with LMD have completely normal CSF.7Common CSF findings include elevated protein level, decreased glucose level, and white blood cell pleocytosis (most commonly lymphocytosis). Although this patient had leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI, these areas did not correspond to her upper extremity neurologic deficits. The unremarkable CSF analysis further excluded paralysis owing to LMD. Although few medications are associated with acute onset quadriparesis, it is important to be mindful of potential drug adverse effects in patients with cancer. Adverse effects associated with ado-trastuzumab emtansine could explain some of the findings in this case, including peripheral neuropathy (shown on electromyogram) and muscle pain, but not paralysis.

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

[Case]
A 39-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer treated with anti-ERBB2 (formerly HER2) chemotherapy (ado-trastuzumab emtansine) presented to the emergency department with acute onset paralysis. Earlier that day she had upper-back muscle spasms while gardening. A few hours later, she developed weakness of both hands and legs, followed by urinary retention and saddle anesthesia. On arrival to the emergency department, the patient was febrile but hemodynamically stable. Speech, comprehension, and cranial nerves were intact. Laboratory test results revealed elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, including white and red blood cell counts, protein and glucose levels, infectious studies, and cytologic testing, was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the total spine showed vertebral body metastases unchanged from a computed tomography scan obtained 8 months prior (Figure 1), multiple areas of new leptomeningeal enhancement around the distal spinal cord, and tumor infiltration of multiple vertebral bodies. An electromyogram showed grossly preserved motor conduction in the upper and lower extremities. F wave latencies (a measure of nerve conduction velocity between the spine and limb) were undetectable in the upper extremities and were normal in the lower extremities, suggesting upper motor neuron disease. Sensory conduction amplitudes of upper and lower extremity peripheral nerves were mildly decreased.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Spinal cord infarct is a devastating syndrome characterized by abrupt symptom onset and accounts for 5% to 8% of acute myelopathy.1At presentation, 72% of patients with spinal cord infarct have associated back or limb pain at the level of involvement. This patient lost motor function and reflexes at the level of the infarct (C6 and C7) and had a loss of sensation at T4, but proprioception and vibratory sensation were maintained throughout the spine. These are hallmark examination findings of disruption of the anterior spinal artery, which supplies the anterior (but not posterior) spinal columns. The cervical plexus (C1 through C4) likely provided redundant innervation to the patient’s upper trunk, accounting for the T4 sensory deficit distal to the infarct. Only 24% of patients with spinal cord infarct have an abnormal MRI at the time of presentation, with most infarctions appearing as myelomalacia (radiographic “softening” of the spinal cord) on subsequent imaging (Figure 2).2Spinal cord infarct is thus largely a clinical diagnosis. Although more typically a result of a perioperative complication, this patient’s anterior spinal artery was likely disrupted by either direct invasion by breast cancer or by a thromboembolic event. Spinal cord infarct is treated with supportive care and reversal of the inciting process when possible. This patient was treated with oral and intrathecal chemotherapy, anticoagulation, and physical therapy; she had modest improvement in strength during a 2-month period. Spinal cord infarct has an estimated 3-year mortality rate of 23% and a wheelchair dependence rate of 42%.3 Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acquired autoimmune peripheral demyelinating disease. This uncommon syndrome (incidence of 1 to 2 per 100 000 people) can be triggered by infection and hematologic cancer.4Weakness owing to GBS progresses over weeks in an ascending fashion, with absent deep tendon reflexes seen in virtually all patients. Cerebrospinal fluid cytoalbuminologic dissociation (elevation of protein level with normal white blood cell count) is present in approximately two-thirds of patients with GBS and may take 1 week to develop. Although this patient was areflexic, the acute onset of her symptoms and preserved motor conduction on electromyogram do not support a diagnosis of GBS. Leptomeningeal disease (LMD) is found at autopsy in 20% of patients with metastatic cancer, and breast cancer is the solid tumor most likely to spread to the leptomeninges.5Multiple areas of involvement are common, and presenting symptoms, which correspond to areas of spinal involvement, are often heterogenous and multifocal. Spine MRI is 76% sensitive for the detection of LMD, demonstrating enhancement of the spinal cord or cauda equina.6Cerebrospinal fluid cytologic testing is only 54% sensitive with the first sample; however, only 3% of patients with LMD have completely normal CSF.7Common CSF findings include elevated protein level, decreased glucose level, and white blood cell pleocytosis (most commonly lymphocytosis). Although this patient had leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI, these areas did not correspond to her upper extremity neurologic deficits. The unremarkable CSF analysis further excluded paralysis owing to LMD. Although few medications are associated with acute onset quadriparesis, it is important to be mindful of potential drug adverse effects in patients with cancer. Adverse effects associated with ado-trastuzumab emtansine could explain some of the findings in this case, including peripheral neuropathy (shown on electromyogram) and muscle pain, but not paralysis.

case_info.scenario: A 39-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer treated with anti-ERBB2 (formerly HER2) chemotherapy (ado-trastuzumab emtansine) presented to the emergency department with acute onset paralysis. Earlier that day she had upper-back muscle spasms while gardening. A few hours later, she developed weakness of both hands and legs, followed by urinary retention and saddle anesthesia. On arrival to the emergency department, the patient was febrile but hemodynamically stable. On physical examination, she had areflexia and weakness affecting all 4 limbs, with a sensory deficit distal to the T4 dermatome. Proprioception and vibratory sensation were intact throughout. Speech, comprehension, and cranial nerves were intact. Laboratory test results revealed elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, including white and red blood cell counts, protein and glucose levels, infectious studies, and cytologic testing, was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the total spine showed vertebral body metastases unchanged from a computed tomography scan obtained 8 months prior (Figure 1), multiple areas of new leptomeningeal enhancement around the distal spinal cord, and tumor infiltration of multiple vertebral bodies. An electromyogram showed grossly preserved motor conduction in the upper and lower extremities. F wave latencies (a measure of nerve conduction velocity between the spine and limb) were undetectable in the upper extremities and were normal in the lower extremities, suggesting upper motor neuron disease. Sensory conduction amplitudes of upper and lower extremity peripheral nerves were mildly decreased.
case_info.caption: A sagittal magnetic resonance imaging scan with contrast shows areas of metastatic breast cancer to the lumbar vertebral bodies, and the arrowheads show leptomeningeal spread.
case_info.explanation: Spinal cord infarct is a devastating syndrome characterized by abrupt symptom onset and accounts for 5% to 8% of acute myelopathy.1At presentation, 72% of patients with spinal cord infarct have associated back or limb pain at the level of involvement. This patient lost motor function and reflexes at the level of the infarct (C6 and C7) and had a loss of sensation at T4, but proprioception and vibratory sensation were maintained throughout the spine. These are hallmark examination findings of disruption of the anterior spinal artery, which supplies the anterior (but not posterior) spinal columns. The cervical plexus (C1 through C4) likely provided redundant innervation to the patient’s upper trunk, accounting for the T4 sensory deficit distal to the infarct. Only 24% of patients with spinal cord infarct have an abnormal MRI at the time of presentation, with most infarctions appearing as myelomalacia (radiographic “softening” of the spinal cord) on subsequent imaging (Figure 2).2Spinal cord infarct is thus largely a clinical diagnosis. Although more typically a result of a perioperative complication, this patient’s anterior spinal artery was likely disrupted by either direct invasion by breast cancer or by a thromboembolic event. Spinal cord infarct is treated with supportive care and reversal of the inciting process when possible. This patient was treated with oral and intrathecal chemotherapy, anticoagulation, and physical therapy; she had modest improvement in strength during a 2-month period. Spinal cord infarct has an estimated 3-year mortality rate of 23% and a wheelchair dependence rate of 42%.3 Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acquired autoimmune peripheral demyelinating disease. This uncommon syndrome (incidence of 1 to 2 per 100 000 people) can be triggered by infection and hematologic cancer.4Weakness owing to GBS progresses over weeks in an ascending fashion, with absent deep tendon reflexes seen in virtually all patients. Cerebrospinal fluid cytoalbuminologic dissociation (elevation of protein level with normal white blood cell count) is present in approximately two-thirds of patients with GBS and may take 1 week to develop. Although this patient was areflexic, the acute onset of her symptoms and preserved motor conduction on electromyogram do not support a diagnosis of GBS. Leptomeningeal disease (LMD) is found at autopsy in 20% of patients with metastatic cancer, and breast cancer is the solid tumor most likely to spread to the leptomeninges.5Multiple areas of involvement are common, and presenting symptoms, which correspond to areas of spinal involvement, are often heterogenous and multifocal. Spine MRI is 76% sensitive for the detection of LMD, demonstrating enhancement of the spinal cord or cauda equina.6Cerebrospinal fluid cytologic testing is only 54% sensitive with the first sample; however, only 3% of patients with LMD have completely normal CSF.7Common CSF findings include elevated protein level, decreased glucose level, and white blood cell pleocytosis (most commonly lymphocytosis). Although this patient had leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI, these areas did not correspond to her upper extremity neurologic deficits. The unremarkable CSF analysis further excluded paralysis owing to LMD. Although few medications are associated with acute onset quadriparesis, it is important to be mindful of potential drug adverse effects in patients with cancer. Adverse effects associated with ado-trastuzumab emtansine could explain some of the findings in this case, including peripheral neuropathy (shown on electromyogram) and muscle pain, but not paralysis.

Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Spinal cord infarct is a devastating syndrome characterized by abrupt symptom onset and accounts for 5% to 8% of acute myelopathy.1At presentation, 72% of patients with spinal cord infarct have associated back or limb pain at the level of involvement. This patient lost motor function and reflexes at the level of the infarct (C6 and C7) and had a loss of sensation at T4, but proprioception and vibratory sensation were maintained throughout the spine. These are hallmark examination findings of disruption of the anterior spinal artery, which supplies the anterior (but not posterior) spinal columns. The cervical plexus (C1 through C4) likely provided redundant innervation to the patient’s upper trunk, accounting for the T4 sensory deficit distal to the infarct. Only 24% of patients with spinal cord infarct have an abnormal MRI at the time of presentation, with most infarctions appearing as myelomalacia (radiographic “softening” of the spinal cord) on subsequent imaging (Figure 2).2Spinal cord infarct is thus largely a clinical diagnosis. Although more typically a result of a perioperative complication, this patient’s anterior spinal artery was likely disrupted by either direct invasion by breast cancer or by a thromboembolic event. Spinal cord infarct is treated with supportive care and reversal of the inciting process when possible. This patient was treated with oral and intrathecal chemotherapy, anticoagulation, and physical therapy; she had modest improvement in strength during a 2-month period. Spinal cord infarct has an estimated 3-year mortality rate of 23% and a wheelchair dependence rate of 42%.3 Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acquired autoimmune peripheral demyelinating disease. This uncommon syndrome (incidence of 1 to 2 per 100 000 people) can be triggered by infection and hematologic cancer.4Weakness owing to GBS progresses over weeks in an ascending fashion, with absent deep tendon reflexes seen in virtually all patients. Cerebrospinal fluid cytoalbuminologic dissociation (elevation of protein level with normal white blood cell count) is present in approximately two-thirds of patients with GBS and may take 1 week to develop. Although this patient was areflexic, the acute onset of her symptoms and preserved motor conduction on electromyogram do not support a diagnosis of GBS. Leptomeningeal disease (LMD) is found at autopsy in 20% of patients with metastatic cancer, and breast cancer is the solid tumor most likely to spread to the leptomeninges.5Multiple areas of involvement are common, and presenting symptoms, which correspond to areas of spinal involvement, are often heterogenous and multifocal. case_info.explanation: Spinal cord infarct is a devastating syndrome characterized by abrupt symptom onset and accounts for 5% to 8% of acute myelopathy.1At presentation, 72% of patients with spinal cord infarct have associated back or limb pain at the level of involvement. This patient lost motor function and reflexes at the level of the infarct (C6 and C7) and had a loss of sensation at T4, but proprioception and vibratory sensation were maintained throughout the spine. These are hallmark examination findings of disruption of the anterior spinal artery, which supplies the anterior (but not posterior) spinal columns. The cervical plexus (C1 through C4) likely provided redundant innervation to the patient’s upper trunk, accounting for the T4 sensory deficit distal to the infarct. Only 24% of patients with spinal cord infarct have an abnormal MRI at the time of presentation, with most infarctions appearing as myelomalacia (radiographic “softening” of the spinal cord) on subsequent imaging (Figure 2).2Spinal cord infarct is thus largely a clinical diagnosis. Although more typically a result of a perioperative complication, this patient’s anterior spinal artery was likely disrupted by either direct invasion by breast cancer or by a thromboembolic event. Spinal cord infarct is treated with supportive care and reversal of the inciting process when possible. This patient was treated with oral and intrathecal chemotherapy, anticoagulation, and physical therapy; she had modest improvement in strength during a 2-month period. Spinal cord infarct has an estimated 3-year mortality rate of 23% and a wheelchair dependence rate of 42%.3 Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acquired autoimmune peripheral demyelinating disease. This uncommon syndrome (incidence of 1 to 2 per 100 000 people) can be triggered by infection and hematologic cancer.4Weakness owing to GBS progresses over weeks in an ascending fashion, with absent deep tendon reflexes seen in virtually all patients. Cerebrospinal fluid cytoalbuminologic dissociation (elevation of protein level with normal white blood cell count) is present in approximately two-thirds of patients with GBS and may take 1 week to develop. Although this patient was areflexic, the acute onset of her symptoms and preserved motor conduction on electromyogram do not support a diagnosis of GBS. Leptomeningeal disease (LMD) is found at autopsy in 20% of patients with metastatic cancer, and breast cancer is the solid tumor most likely to spread to the leptomeninges.5Multiple areas of involvement are common, and presenting symptoms, which correspond to areas of spinal involvement, are often heterogenous and multifocal. Spine MRI is 76% sensitive for the detection of LMD, demonstrating enhancement of the spinal cord or cauda equina.6Cerebrospinal fluid cytologic testing is only 54% sensitive with the first sample; however, only 3% of patients with LMD have completely normal CSF.7Common CSF findings include elevated protein level, decreased glucose level, and white blood cell pleocytosis (most commonly lymphocytosis). [Case]
A 39-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer treated with anti-ERBB2 (formerly HER2) chemotherapy (ado-trastuzumab emtansine) presented to the emergency department with acute onset paralysis. Earlier that day she had upper-back muscle spasms while gardening. A few hours later, she developed weakness of both hands and legs, followed by urinary retention and saddle anesthesia. On arrival to the emergency department, the patient was febrile but hemodynamically stable. On physical examination, she had areflexia and weakness affecting all 4 limbs, with a sensory deficit distal to the T4 dermatome. Proprioception and vibratory sensation were intact throughout. Speech, comprehension, and cranial nerves were intact. Laboratory test results revealed elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, including white and red blood cell counts, protein and glucose levels, infectious studies, and cytologic testing, was unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the total spine showed vertebral body metastases unchanged from a computed tomography scan obtained 8 months prior (Figure 1), multiple areas of new leptomeningeal enhancement around the distal spinal cord, and tumor infiltration of multiple vertebral bodies. An electromyogram showed grossly preserved motor conduction in the upper and lower extremities. F wave latencies (a measure of nerve conduction velocity between the spine and limb) were undetectable in the upper extremities and were normal in the lower extremities, suggesting upper motor neuron disease. Sensory conduction amplitudes of upper and lower extremity peripheral nerves were mildly decreased.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.
